title: Sore Throat, Again
subtitle: A young man with repeated sore throats, from the first visit to six weeks after surgery
description: The frequency criteria, what counts as a documented episode, reading a neck CT, what to tell an adult about recovery, discharge analgesia, and what the largest adult trial says about the benefit.

steps.title: Step 1/6: The Criteria
steps.scenario:
A 25-year-old man comes to clinic with recurrent tonsillitis. For the past two years he has had repeated episodes of severe sore throat with fever and pus on the tonsils, and courses of antibiotics from several clinics have not stopped them coming back.

On examination both tonsils are grade III.
steps.question: When you discuss surgery with him, you refer to the Paradise criteria. Which frequency of episodes meets the criteria for tonsillectomy?

options.text: (A) Three episodes in the past six months
(B) At least 7 in one year; or at least 5 per year for two years; or at least 3 per year for three years
(C) A single episode with fever
(D) At least 5 in one year

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The three thresholds come from the Paradise trial: 7 or more episodes in the past year, or 5 or more per year for two years, or 3 or more per year for three years. Any one of the three is enough. The UK guideline (SIGN) uses the same numbers for adults and adds that the episodes must be disabling and prevent normal functioning. The NATTINA trial, the largest adult tonsillectomy trial, used exactly these entry criteria.

Why the others fail:
(A) Three in six months is a high rate, but the criteria count full years, and three in six months does not reach any of the three thresholds.
(C) One episode is never an indication, however severe.
(D) Five in one year falls short. Five per year counts only when it happens two years running.

Keypoint: 7 in one year, 5 a year for two years, or 3 a year for three years.

Reference: Paradise JL, Bluestone CD, Bachman RZ, et al. Efficacy of tonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection in severely affected children: results of parallel randomized and nonrandomized clinical trials. N Engl J Med. 1984;310(11):674-683. doi:10.1056/NEJM198403153101102. Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network. Management of Sore Throat and Indications for Tonsillectomy. SIGN publication no. 117. Edinburgh: SIGN; 2010.

steps.title: Step 2/6: What Counts
steps.scenario:
He says there have been more than ten episodes this year. You open the chart to count them.

To count toward the criteria, an episode has to be documented at the time it happened.
steps.question: Which of these counts as a documented episode?

options.text: (A) A phone call to the clinic for sore throat, with antibiotics prescribed
(B) A sore throat he reports at a later visit
(C) A sore throat with at least one of: temperature above 38.3 C, cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or a positive strep test recorded at that visit
(D) A sore throat with a normal examination and no fever recorded

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

An episode counts only when the note from that visit records a sore throat plus at least one of four findings: temperature above 38.3 C (101 F), cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or a positive test for group A streptococcus.

His chart has nine visits for sore throat this year. Seven have one of those findings recorded. Two say only "sore throat, antibiotic prescribed." So he has seven documented episodes, which meets the first threshold.

Why the others fail:
(A) Nothing was examined or measured, so nothing can be counted.
(B) Recall is not documentation. The requirement exists because the trials that showed benefit enrolled patients whose episodes had these recorded features.
(D) A sore throat with a normal examination is most likely viral, and it is not one of the episodes the trials counted.

Keypoint: count what the chart recorded at the time, not what the patient remembers.

Reference: Paradise JL, Bluestone CD, Bachman RZ, et al. Efficacy of tonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection in severely affected children: results of parallel randomized and nonrandomized clinical trials. N Engl J Med. 1984;310(11):674-683. doi:10.1056/NEJM198403153101102. Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network. Management of Sore Throat and Indications for Tonsillectomy. SIGN publication no. 117. Edinburgh: SIGN; 2010.

steps.title: Step 3/6: The CT
steps.scenario:
Two months ago, during his worst episode, he went to the emergency department with a muffled voice, difficulty opening his mouth, and swelling on the left side of the throat. The emergency physician obtained a contrast-enhanced CT of the neck.

You pull up the scan.
steps.media: Load image: Axial contrast-enhanced CT of the neck at the level of the oropharynx, unannotated. Caption: 'Axial, post-contrast.'
steps.question: What does the CT show, and what was the right treatment at that visit?

options.text: (A) Peritonsillar cellulitis without a collection; intravenous antibiotics alone
(B) Retropharyngeal abscess; drainage through the neck under general anesthesia
(C) Parapharyngeal abscess; drainage through the neck under general anesthesia
(D) Peritonsillar abscess; needle aspiration or incision and drainage, plus antibiotics

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The CT shows a rim-enhancing fluid collection between the tonsil and the superior constrictor muscle, with the tonsil pushed medially. That is a peritonsillar abscess. Once a collection has formed, antibiotics alone are not enough: it has to be drained. Needle aspiration and incision and drainage give similar results, and both are done in the emergency department or clinic under local anesthesia in a cooperative adult.

Why the others fail:
(A) Cellulitis and abscess look similar from the outside. The CT is what separates them. A rim-enhancing collection means pus, and pus is drained.
(B) A retropharyngeal abscess sits behind the pharynx, in front of the prevertebral fascia, and is a different picture on CT. It is also uncommon in adults.
(C) A parapharyngeal abscess sits lateral to the constrictor muscle, near the carotid sheath, and needs drainage through the neck. This collection is medial to the constrictor.

One peritonsillar abscess on top of recurrent tonsillitis is an additional reason to offer tonsillectomy, and after two abscesses the case for surgery is strong on its own.

Keypoint: a rim-enhancing collection is drained; where it sits decides how.

Reference: Powell J, Wilson JA. An evidence-based review of peritonsillar abscess. Clin Otolaryngol. 2012;37(2):136-145.

steps.title: Step 4/6: What Recovery Looks Like
steps.scenario:
Seven documented episodes in one year meets the criteria, and he wants surgery. Before booking it you talk about recovery.

He works full time and asks how long he will be off.
steps.question: What do you tell him about recovery in an adult?

options.text: (A) Pain is worse and lasts longer than in children, usually around two weeks, and about one in five adults in the largest trial reported some postoperative bleeding
(B) Recovery is like a child's: two or three days of discomfort and back to work within a week
(C) Bleeding is rare in adults because the tonsillar bed is larger and easier to cauterize
(D) He should expect to stay in hospital for several days

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Adults have more pain after tonsillectomy than children and it lasts longer, usually about two weeks. In NATTINA, 39 percent of participants had an adverse event related to the surgery, and the most common was bleeding, reported by 19 percent. That is higher than older reports of 5 to 10 percent, partly because the trial contacted patients proactively to ask. Plan two weeks off work and tell him what a bleed looks like and where to go.

Why the others fail:
(B) This is the child's course, and adults do worse on every measure: pain, time to eating normally, and days off.
(C) The opposite of the evidence. Adult bleeding rates are higher than children's, not lower.
(D) Uncomplicated adult tonsillectomy is a day case or overnight stay. Several days is not expected.

Keypoint: two weeks of significant pain, and a real bleeding risk he needs to be told about before he agrees.

Reference: Wilson JA, O'Hara J, Fouweather T, et al. Conservative management versus tonsillectomy in adults with recurrent acute tonsillitis in the UK (NATTINA). Lancet. 2023;401(10393):2051-2059. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(23)00519-6.

steps.title: Step 5/6: Going Home
steps.scenario: The operation is uncomplicated. He received a single intraoperative dose of dexamethasone and no perioperative antibiotics. He is ready to go home the same evening and asks what to take for the pain.
steps.question: What do you prescribe?

options.text: (A) An opioid alone, since anti-inflammatory drugs increase the risk of bleeding
(B) Scheduled acetaminophen and ibuprofen, with a small supply of an opioid only for breakthrough pain
(C) Acetaminophen alone, since ibuprofen increases the risk of bleeding
(D) A course of antibiotics, which reduces pain by reducing bacterial load in the tonsillar bed

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Scheduled acetaminophen and ibuprofen together are the base of pain control, taken by the clock for the first week rather than as needed. Adult pain is severe enough that a short supply of an opioid for breakthrough is reasonable, with a set number of tablets and no refill.

Why the others fail:
(A) Ibuprofen has not been shown to increase post-tonsillectomy bleeding that requires intervention. Leaving it out means more opioid, not less bleeding.
(C) Same error. Withholding ibuprofen weakens the regimen without lowering the bleeding risk.
(D) Antibiotics do not reduce post-tonsillectomy pain. The Cochrane review from Step 4 covers this directly.

Keypoint: acetaminophen and ibuprofen by the clock, opioid only for breakthrough.

Reference: Dhiwakar M, Clement WA, Supriya M, McKerrow W. Antibiotics to reduce post-tonsillectomy morbidity. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;12(12):CD005607. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD005607.pub4. Mitchell RB, Archer SM, Ishman SL, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2019;160(1_suppl):S1-S42, Key Action Statement 13.

steps.title: Step 6/6: Six Weeks Later
steps.scenario:
The fossae are healed and there was no bleeding. He is back at work.

He asks whether this means the sore throats are over.
steps.question: What do you tell him?

options.text: (A) He should not get sore throats again, since the tonsils have been removed
(B) Tonsillectomy has not been shown to help adults, and it was done to make each episode milder
(C) He will have fewer sore throat days, not none: in the largest adult trial, about 23 days over two years compared with 30 without surgery
(D) His immune defenses are now weaker, so he should expect more infections of other kinds

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

NATTINA randomized 453 adults who met the criteria to tonsillectomy or conservative management and counted sore throat days for two years. The tonsillectomy group had a median of 23 days against 30 in the conservative group, and after adjustment the rate was about half. The surgery was also cost-effective. So the benefit is real, but it is fewer days, not zero.

Why the others fail:
(A) Removing the tonsils does not remove the pharynx. He can still get pharyngitis, including streptococcal pharyngitis.
(B) Wrong on both counts. NATTINA showed a clear reduction in sore throat days, and the operation was done for frequency, not for severity of individual episodes.
(D) No study has shown a clinically meaningful effect of tonsillectomy on immune function.

Keypoint: about half the sore throat days, not none of them.

Reference: Wilson JA, O'Hara J, Fouweather T, et al. Lancet. 2023;401(10393):2051-2059. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(23)00519-6.
